opus-5.5.text:
I think about this as two complementary sources, but if you ask me about the long term, I'm quite bullish on simulation.

Real data has one huge advantage: it's real. There's no sim-to-real gap. When you collect teleoperation data on a physical robot, the contacts, the friction, the sensor noise are all exactly what the robot will see when it's deployed. That's why so much of the recent progress in robot foundation models has come from large-scale real-world data collection. But real data is expensive, slow, and hard to scale. You need physical robots, human operators, resets, maintenance. And it's very hard to collect the long tail: the dangerous situations, the rare failures, the edge cases where you actually most want the robot to learn.

Simulation is the opposite. It's cheap, it's parallel, and you can run thousands of environments faster than real time. You can randomize everything: lighting, textures, masses, friction. And you can create scenarios that would be unsafe or impractical in the real world. We've seen how powerful this is for locomotion. Most of the agile legged locomotion you see today was trained almost entirely in simulation with reinforcement learning and transferred zero-shot or close to it. That was something people thought was very hard ten years ago.

The challenge is manipulation, especially contact-rich manipulation with deformable objects, liquids, cloth, and complex visual scenes. Physics engines and renderers are still not good enough there, and creating diverse, realistic assets and tasks at scale is a lot of manual work. That's where the gap remains.

But I think several trends are changing this. First, simulators keep getting better: faster, more accurate, differentiable, GPU-accelerated. Second, generative models are starting to help build simulation content, generating 3D assets, scenes, even tasks and reward functions automatically, which addresses the content bottleneck. And third, world models learned from video could act as a kind of learned simulator, where the boundary between "simulation" and "data" starts to blur.

So my view is that in the near term, real data will continue to be critical, especially for manipulation and for grounding. In the long term, the volume of data needed to reach truly general-purpose robots is so large that it's hard to imagine getting there with real data alone. Simulation, whether physics-based, learned, or a hybrid, will provide the bulk of the experience, and real data will be used more for calibration, fine-tuning, and closing the final gap. Similar to how humans learn a lot through imagination and mental rehearsal, but still need real practice to get it right.

r001.rationale: The response says the data required for general-purpose robots is too large to obtain from real data alone, and describes real-world collection as expensive, slow, and hard to scale.

r002.rationale: It identifies a sim-to-real gap, especially for manipulation, but does not explain that the gap can obscure gains from increasing simulation training data.

r003.rationale: It describes improving simulators and learned world models, but does not state that a research breakthrough could remove an apparent performance ceiling in simulation-based training.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. This is a question I've spent most of my career thinking about, so let me try to give you an honest answer rather than a slogan.

I'm very bullish on simulation in the long run, but I want to be precise about why. Robotics has a data problem that's fundamentally different from language or vision. The internet gave us trillions of tokens of text and billions of images essentially for free. There is no internet of robot actions. Every real-world trajectory costs money, time, hardware wear, and often a human teleoperator standing there for hours. Even the most ambitious real-data efforts today collect on the order of thousands of hours, and that's a rounding error compared to what pretraining in other domains uses.

Simulation breaks that scaling bottleneck. You can run thousands of environments in parallel on a single GPU, randomize physics, lighting, object geometry, and you get effectively unlimited data at near-zero marginal cost. We saw this in legged locomotion. The robots that walk robustly across ice, stairs, and rubble today were almost entirely trained in simulation. A few years ago people said sim-to-real would never work for contact-rich dynamics, and that turned out to be wrong.

That said, I don't think simulation replaces real data. I think of them as covering different parts of the problem. Simulation is excellent for physics, for control, for the low-level question of "how do I move my body." It is much weaker on the long tail of the visual and semantic world. Deformable objects, liquids, transparent surfaces, cluttered kitchens that nobody modeled. Real data captures that messiness for free, precisely because you didn't have to specify it.

So the pattern I expect to win is a loop rather than a choice. Real data tells you where the simulator is wrong and calibrates it. Simulation lets you amplify that real data by orders of magnitude and explore failure cases you'd never dare to collect physically. And increasingly, generative models blur the line entirely. If a world model can produce realistic video of a robot's future given its actions, is that simulation or synthetic real data? I think that distinction will matter less and less.

If you forced me to put numbers on it, I'd say the fraction of training data that is simulated or synthetic for a capable general-purpose robot will be well above ninety percent. But the small real slice will be disproportionately valuable, because it's the thing anchoring everything else to reality. The teams that succeed will be the ones who get good at both and understand exactly what each one is for.

r001.rationale: It says real robot trajectories are costly and that even ambitious collection is only thousands of hours, a rounding error versus other domains, identifying a real-data scaling bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It discusses simulation’s weaknesses and the need for real data to calibrate it, but does not say that the sim-to-real gap can hide gains from adding more simulation training data.

r003.rationale: It notes that sim-to-real once seemed impossible but proved workable; it does not suggest a research breakthrough could lift a performance ceiling in simulation-based training.

astra-6.text:
I think simulation has enormous long-term potential, but I don’t see it as a complete replacement for real-world data. The two are complementary.

Simulation gives you scale. You can run many robots in parallel, explore different environments, and let them fail without damaging hardware. That’s particularly valuable for learning through trial and error. But you’re always learning inside an approximation of the world. If the simulator gets an important interaction wrong, the robot may learn a strategy that works beautifully in simulation and fails in reality.

Real data helps close that gap. You can use it to improve the simulator, identify what you’re missing, and adapt the policy to the actual robot. So I see a cycle: collect real data, improve simulation, train at scale, and then test in the real world.

Over time, I expect more of the training experience to come from simulation. But the amount of simulated data isn’t the only thing that matters. The key is whether it captures the variation and physics that matter for the task. Real-world experience will remain the grounding for that.

r001.rationale: The response says real-world experience will remain important, but does not state that real training data will encounter a data wall.

r002.rationale: It notes that simulator inaccuracies can make a learned strategy fail in reality, but does not explain that the sim-to-real gap can obscure gains from adding simulation data.

r003.rationale: The response anticipates more training in simulation, but does not suggest a research breakthrough could remove a performance ceiling.

sol-6.1.text:
I think simulation has tremendous long-term potential because it lets us generate diverse experiences at a scale that would be very difficult to achieve with real robots. We can run many robots in parallel, vary the environment, and let them practice failures that would be expensive or unsafe in the real world.

But the important question is not just how much data we can generate. It is whether that data helps a robot perform in reality. A policy can become very good at exploiting the simulator’s inaccuracies, so more simulated data does not automatically mean better real-world performance.

I see simulation and real data as complementary. Real data can help us identify where the simulator is wrong and ground our models in reality. Simulation can then expand the range of situations the robot experiences. Over time, I expect simulation to provide a large share of training experience, while real-world testing and data remain essential for validating and improving what the robot learns.
